metadata.title: Elasto-Visco-Plastic-Damage Model for Pre-Strained 304L Stainless Steel Subjected to Low Temperature
metadata.description: Primary barrier of membrane type LNG containment system consist of corrugated 304L stainless steel. This 304L stainless steel is austenitic stainless steel which shows different material behaviors owing to phase transformation during the plastic work. Even though corrugated primary barriers are subjected to significant amounts of pre-strain due to press working, quantitative mechanical behavior on the effect of pre-straining at cryogenic temperatures are not available. In this study, pre-strain level and pre-strain temperature dependent tensile tests are carried to investigate mechanical behaviors. Also, constitutive equations with material parameters are suggested for a verification study.

metadata.title: HE-Austenite: Hydrogen Embrittlement of Austenitic Stainless Steels in Gaseous Hydrogen, Separating Weld Metal from Base metal, with Per-Heat Composition
metadata.description:
Hydrogen Embrittlement in Austenetic Stainless Steels: an open dataset of hydrogen embrittlement in austenitic stainless steels in gaseous hydrogen, with weld zone and per-heat composition

 An open dataset of hydrogen embrittlement in austenitic stainless steels tested in hydrogen gas, with the weld zone and the published composition recorded for every record.

113 records · 45 fields · 9 sources, 1983–2024 · Data CC BY 4.0 · Code MIT

Values were extracted by hand from published tables. No new experiments were performed, and no source document is redistributed here.

Objective

Hydrogen infrastructure is welded. Refuelling stations run at 70 MPa, storage vessels and tube trailers are welded assemblies, and repurposing existing pipe networks depends on how the joints behave rather than the plate. A weld is a casting sitting inside a wrought product: dendritic, different in composition from the parent metal, and deliberately holding a few percent of delta ferrite to avoid solidification cracking. It is the part of a joint least like the material a designer looked up, and the part hydrogen reaches first.

Most published embrittlement data covers base metal, and most recent weld studies charge specimens electrochemically, which cannot be converted to an equivalent gas pressure without assumptions about charging efficiency. This dataset keeps only gaseous exposure and records the weld zone for every row.

SCOPE

A record is included when the material is an austenitic stainless steel or a related grade flagged by material_family (duplex 2507, A286); hydrogen was introduced as a gas, either by testing in high-pressure hydrogen or by thermal precharging in hydrogen gas; a reference measurement exists from the same study and material, in air, helium, nitrogen, argon or the uncharged condition; and the value appears in a table rather than only in a figure.

Coverage: 228 to 423 K, and 0.1 to 172 MPa hydrogen for the 104 records whose source stated a pressure.

Electrochemically charged studies are excluded, because hydrogen fugacity from cathodic charging cannot be converted to an equivalent gas pressure without assumptions. They are listed with the reason in the Extraction log sheet of the workbook, alongside sources identified too late for this release.

WHAT ONE RECORD IS

One record is one reported test condition and one property: an alloy and heat, a weld zone, a hydrogen exposure, a test temperature and strain rate, the property measured in the reference environment, the property measured in or after hydrogen, and the ratio of the two. Where the property is reduction of area, that ratio is the relative reduction of area, RRA.

WHAT IS IN THIS VERSION

Per-heat composition for 102 of 113 records, as ten element columns in weight percent, with composition_basis saying whether the value is a measured heat analysis or a nominal composition, and composition_source naming the exact table it was read from. A composition is attached to a record only when the source reports it for the same heat, weld deposit or filler as the mechanical test, and a specification range is never recorded as a measurement.

A nickel equivalent recomputed for every record from one expression, Hirayama's six-element form, Ni + 0.65 Cr + 0.98 Mo + 1.05 Mn + 0.35 Si + 12.6 C, covering 93 records. Where a source printed its own value on a different expression it is kept separately in ni_equivalent_reported rather than mixed into the recomputed column.

Angel Md30 for the 55 records whose composition falls inside the range that expression was fitted on. Outside that range the linear form returns temperatures below absolute zero, which is a sign that it does not apply rather than a measure of stability, so it is not computed there.

The recomputed nickel equivalent reproduces four values the sources themselves print — Nakamura et al. (2018) heats P and a, and Fukunaga (2024) SUS316CW and A286 — exactly.

WHAT THE DATA SHOWS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

Relative reduction of area is the value measured in or after hydrogen divided by the value in the reference environment. A value of 1.0 means no measurable loss. Japanese regulatory practice accepts austenitic stainless steels for hydrogen service at RRA greater than or equal to 0.80.

Zone and alloy family are not independent in this dataset, so they have to be read together. Pooled across all families, base metal sits at a median RRA of 0.85 over 36 records and weld metal at 0.49 over 14, but those two groups are not comparable head to head: the weld-metal records come from three sources and 12 of the 14 are type 304 family, while the base-metal records span eight families and include the more stable grades. Within the type 304 family the comparison is 0.72 against 0.48, and within types 316 and 317 it is 0.99 against 0.73 on two weld records.

Ductility retained rises with the nickel equivalent: Spearman rho = 0.60 across the 24 distinct heats, weld deposits and fillers behind the 54 reduction-of-area records that carry a composition, p = 0.002. Statistics are quoted per material rather than per record because eight of the Sandia composite weld rows share a single fusion-zone analysis. The criterion Ni_eq greater than or equal to 26.3, proposed by Matsuoka et al., separates 10 materials at a median RRA of 0.64 from 14 at 0.95.

That relationship holds between alloy families and not within one. The low band is 26 of 27 records from the type 304 family, and within that family alone, where nine materials span Ni_eq 23.0 to 26.5, the relationship disappears, rho = -0.12, p = 0.77. It is not an artefact of the mixed reference environments: restricting to air and helium references leaves rho = 0.63 across 18 materials, p = 0.005. Md30 carries no relationship with ductility retained inside its valid range, rho = -0.42, p = 0.13.

Welds sit below base metal inside both nickel-equivalent bands, 0.71 against 0.47 below 26.3 and 0.99 against 0.86 at or above it, which argues that the zone effect is not only a composition effect. Each weld cell rests on three weld deposits, so this is a direction worth testing rather than a quantity worth citing.

DELTA FERRITE

Nakamura et al. (2018) tested one TIG-welded bar three ways at 228 K in 106 MPa hydrogen against a nitrogen reference: 316 high-nickel base metal at RRA 1.02, 317L weld metal as welded at 0.55, and the same weld metal after a post-weld solution treatment at 0.91. One material, one gas, one temperature, with the treatment that dissolves the ferrite as the variable.

This reading is contested and the dataset cannot settle it. Hirata (2015) reports RRA against delta ferrite ratio for ten weld metals in 45 MPa hydrogen gas and concludes the opposite, that weld-metal embrittlement is governed by austenite stability rather than by delta ferrite. That study reports its results only in figures and is therefore not included here. The ferrite_number field is populated for 2 of 113 records, so nobody should model ferrite content against ductility from this release.

KNOWN LIMITS

Identification, screening and extraction were done by one person. There was no second independent screener, so screening error cannot be quantified. 24 of 113 records were independently re-extracted from the source documents and matched; those rows are marked verified = yes.

The heat affected zone and the fusion line are defined in the zone vocabulary but carry no records.

Reference environments are mixed: 48 records against air, 28 against high-pressure helium, 32 against the uncharged condition, 5 against nitrogen or argon. A helium reference at test pressure is stricter than an air reference, and the field is recorded so users can filter. Twelve of the 14 weld-metal records use an uncharged reference.

Eleven records carry no composition because their source names no heat; they are left empty rather than filled from a specification.

The Sandia 304L heat W69 is published with C = 0.20 wt%, far outside the 304L specification and almost certainly a typographical error in the source. It is recorded as printed and flagged, and it raises that heat's nickel equivalent by about 2.2. One record uses it.

Weld compositions are the fusion zone or filler analysis the source gives. Dilution of the filler by the parent plate is not accounted for anywhere, because no source in this set reports it.

Family medians for types 321 and 347 (n = 3), type 310 (n = 2), duplex (n = 2) and A286 (n = 1) rest on few records and are indicative only.

SOURCES

San Marchi C, Somerday BP (eds). Technical Reference on Hydrogen Compatibility of Materials. SAND2012-7321, Sandia National Laboratories, 2012. https://h2tools.org/technical-reference

Nakamura J, Okazaki S, Matsunaga H, Matsuoka S. SSRT and fatigue life properties of 317L weld metal in high-pressure hydrogen gas. Transactions of the JSME 84(857) 2018, in Japanese. https://doi.org/10.1299/transjsme.17-00437

FILES IN THIS DEPOSIT

he_austenite_v0.2.csv — the dataset, 113 records, 45 fields
HE-Austenite_v0.2.xlsx — the same rows plus summary, data dictionary, sources and extraction log sheets
compositions.csv — one row per heat, weld deposit or filler, with the table each composition came from
record_composition_map.csv — which record uses which composition
records_raw.json — the raw extraction records with full provenance notes
data_dictionary.md — every column, its meaning and its completeness
schema.json — the record schema
normalise.py, apply_compositions.py, build_outputs.py, build_workbook.py, make_figures.py — the pipeline
fig1_family.png, fig2_pressure.png, fig3_ferrite.png, fig4_nieq.png — the figures
README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CITATION.cff, LICENSE, LICENSE-DATA.txt, requirements.txt

The pipeline reproduces the released CSV byte for byte from a clean copy, in the order normalise, apply_compositions, build_outputs, build_workbook, make_figures.

CHANGES FROM THE PREVIOUS VERSION

The first release, deposited in September 2026, carried no composition data and a nickel equivalent for only 14 records. This version adds composition for 102 records, recomputes the nickel equivalent for 93 on a single expression, and adds Md30 for 55. No mechanical property, ratio or record identifier changed, so analysis built on the previous version still runs.

REPOSITORY

https://github.com/mfaizansworkspace-ai/Hydrogen-Embrittlement-in-Austenitic-Stainless-Steels 

Corrections and contributions are welcome. CONTRIBUTING.md gives the column spec, the provenance rules and how credit is handled. If a value here disagrees with the source in front of you, open an issue with the record identifier, the value in the dataset, the value you read and the table it came from.

HOW TO CITE

Faizan, M. (2026). HE-Austenite: hydrogen embrittlement of austenitic stainless
steels in gaseous hydrogen, separating weld metal from base metal, with per-heat
composition (v0.2) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23107694

Numbered style:

M. Faizan, HE-Austenite: Hydrogen Embrittlement of Austenitic Stainless Steels in Gaseous Hydrogen, Separating Weld Metal from Base metal, with Per-Heat Composition
, Zenodo (2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23107694.

10.5281/zenodo.23107694 points to this version and its exact numbers. The concept
DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22922356 always resolves to the newest version; use it when you
mean the dataset in general. If your results depend on the values, cite the version.

CITATION.cff in the repository carries the same details in machine-readable form.

LICENCE

Data files are CC BY 4.0. Code is MIT.

metadata.title: Understanding Physics-Guided Machine Learning: Applications, Trends, and Challenges for Aerospace
metadata.description: The article provides a systematic review of the PGML concept as a new approach to modeling complex engineering problems in aerospace engineering. Particular attention is focused on how the integration of physical laws with machine learning algorithms transforms traditional approaches to analysis, design, and operation of structures. The principles underlying PGML are examined: modification of the loss function to account for residuals of physical equations, constructive embedding of symmetries into the model structure, and the development of a computational space based on physical invariants. The methodology of this work is based on the analysis of four aerospace-related problems: material fatigue prediction, flutter prediction—an aerodynamic phenomenon characterized by unstable self-oscillations of structures—design of thin-walled structures, and structural condition monitoring. Approximately 30 peer-reviewed sources were analyzed, enabling the identification of key directions for implementation in the design and analysis of the aerospace industry. A limitation of the PGML analysis is the limited number of published sources, which may be somewhat superficial. Key PGML implementations — namely PINNs, GAPINN, NSFnet, multi-fidelity, and hybrid models—and their effectiveness in cases of limited data samples are analyzed. Attention is also given to model interpretability issues, including the application of explainable ML, symbolic regression, and Bayesian approaches for solution verification in critical scenarios. The main challenges for widespread PGML adoption are identified: balancing physical and statistical components, scalability limitations in multiphase environments, certification complexity, and instability in solving inverse problems. The study concludes that PGML transcends being a mere application of machine learning and emerges as a new epistemological platform for formulating engineering hypotheses.

Hydrogen infrastructure is welded. Refuelling stations run at 70 MPa, storage vessels and tube trailers are welded assemblies, and repurposing existing pipe networks depends on how the joints behave rather than the plate. A weld is a casting sitting inside a wrought product: dendritic, different in composition from the parent metal, and deliberately holding a few percent of delta ferrite to avoid solidification cracking. It is the part of a joint least like the material a designer looked up, and the part hydrogen reaches first.

Most published embrittlement data covers base metal, and most recent weld studies charge specimens electrochemically, which cannot be converted to an equivalent gas pressure without assumptions about charging efficiency. This dataset keeps only gaseous exposure and records the weld zone for every row.

Scope

A record is included when the material is an austenitic stainless steel or a related grade flagged by material_family (duplex 2507, A286); hydrogen was introduced as a gas, either by testing in high-pressure hydrogen or by thermal precharging in hydrogen gas; a reference measurement exists from the same study and material; and the value appears in a table rather than only in a figure.

Coverage: 228 to 423 K, and 0.1 to 172 MPa hydrogen for the 104 records whose source stated a pressure. Electrochemically charged studies are excluded and logged with the reason.

What is in v0.2

Per-heat composition for 102 of 113 records, as ten element columns with composition_basis (measured heat analysis or nominal composition) and composition_source naming the exact table. A nickel equivalent recomputed for every record from one expression, Hirayama's six-element form, for 93 records; where a source printed its own value on a different expression it is kept separately in ni_equivalent_reported. Angel Md30 for the 55 records whose composition falls inside the range that expression was fitted on.

The recomputed nickel equivalent reproduces four values the sources themselves print — Nakamura et al. (2018) heats P and a, Fukunaga (2024) SUS316CW and A286 — exactly.

What the data shows, and what it does not

Relative reduction of area (RRA) is the value measured in or after hydrogen divided by the value in the reference environment. Japanese regulatory practice accepts austenitic stainless steels for hydrogen service at RRA ≥ 0.80.

Ductility retained rises with the nickel equivalent: Spearman ρ = 0.60 across the 24 distinct heats, weld deposits and fillers behind the 54 reduction-of-area records that carry a composition (p = 0.002). The criterion Ni_eq ≥ 26.3 separates 10 materials at median RRA 0.64 from 14 at 0.95.

That relationship holds between alloy families and not within one. The low band is 26 of 27 records from the type 304 family, and within that family alone, where nine materials span Ni_eq 23.0 to 26.5, the relationship disappears (ρ = −0.12, p = 0.77). Md30 carries no relationship with ductility retained inside its valid range (ρ = −0.42, p = 0.13).

Welds sit below base metal inside both nickel-equivalent bands, 0.71 against 0.47 below 26.3 and 0.99 against 0.86 at or above it, which argues the zone effect is not only a composition effect. Each weld cell rests on three weld deposits, so this is a direction worth testing rather than a quantity worth citing.

Known limits

Identification, screening and extraction were done by one person; 24 of 113 records were independently re-extracted and matched. The heat affected zone and fusion line are defined in the vocabulary but carry no records. Reference environments are mixed (48 air, 28 high-pressure helium, 32 uncharged, 5 nitrogen or argon) and the field is recorded so users can filter. Eleven records carry no composition because their source names no heat; they are left empty rather than filled from a specification. The Sandia 304L heat W69 is published with C = 0.20 wt%, far outside the 304L specification and almost certainly a typographical error in the source; it is recorded as printed and flagged.

Files and code

The structured repository, with the data under data/ and the pipeline under scripts/, is at https://github.com/mfaizansworkspace-ai/Hydrogen-Embrittlement-in-Austenitic-Stainless-Steels

The pipeline reproduces the released CSV byte for byte from a clean clone: normalise.py → apply_compositions.py → build_outputs.py → build_workbook.py → make_figures.py.

Corrections and contributions are welcome; CONTRIBUTING.md gives the column spec, the provenance rules and how credit is handled.

metadata.title: Innovations, Prospects, and Future Directions in Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing
metadata.description:
Abstract: Over the past three decades, extensive research has been conducted on Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM), a production technology with roots dating back almost a century to its initial patent. WAAM has garnered increasing attention due to its ability to fabricate large near-net-shape metal products. Leveraging existing welding equipment for both the heat source and material feedstock provides a significant advantage in terms of lower initial investment costs. Initially prominent in the aerospace sector with a focus on lightweight metal alloys, WAAM has recently expanded its application scope to include stainless steels, functionally graded materials, and combinations of diverse alloys. This study aims to explore the latest advancements and potential pathways in WAAM technology, offering valuable insights and recommendations for future research directions.

metadata.title: Viscoelastic Decoupling of Sulfur-Ceramic Linings for Low-Cost Chemical Bulk Carrier Retrofitting
metadata.description:
This technical memorandum presents a theoretical materials architecture and structural framework for marine chemical transport. The viscoelastic coupling methodology proposed herein is derived from empirical systems-thinking and supported by advanced predictive modeling. As a conceptual framework, the stoichiometric ratios provided act as baseline hypotheses; future institutional wet-lab validation and marine stress-testing are required to establish exact operational parameters. (Note: The intellectual property framework and licensing terms for applied industrial deployment are detailed at the end of this document).

The maritime transport of hyper-saline brines, acidic leachates, and toxic industrial fluids is currently constrained by the prohibitive CAPEX of specialized chemical tankers (stainless steel 316L or advanced epoxy linings). Standard dry bulk carriers cannot be utilized due to rapid chloride/acid-induced hull corrosion. While sulfur concrete provides absolute chemical resistance, its inherent brittleness precludes its use in mobile marine applications subjected to severe hull deflection and torsional stress. This paper introduces a novel structural paradigm: Viscoelastic Decoupling. By separating the chemical shielding function from the mechanical flexibility requirement, we propose a bilayer matrix. A continuous, shock-absorbing sub-layer of modified heavy bitumen acts as an elastic adhesive interface, upon which modular, rigid sulfur-ceramic tiles "float." This architecture neutralizes flexural stress from wave action, rendering the brittle nature of sulfur irrelevant. The system allows end-of-life dry bulk carriers to be retrofitted into specialized chemical/brine tankers at a fraction of standard industry costs, utilizing abundant refinery waste streams (sulfur and bitumen).

Methodological Note & Radical Transparency (Scope of Work):
This technical memorandum presents a theoretical materials architecture and structural framework for marine chemical transport. It is the exclusive product of pure deductive reasoning, cross-disciplinary systems-thinking, and advanced Large Language Model (LLM) synthesis. No physical wet-lab prototyping, shipyard retrofitting, or marine stress-testing has been conducted by the author to generate these specific metrics. The stoichiometric ratios and structural methodologies proposed herein are predictive baseline hypotheses derived from the strict application of materials science and naval architecture principles. Consequently, institutional wet-lab validation and classification society stress-testing (e.g., Lloyd's Register) remain absolutely required to establish exact operational parameters prior to commercial deployment.

metadata.title: Révolution des échangeurs à CO2 supercritique par optimisation fractale : Application au parc nucléaire français
metadata.description:
Title: Hybrid sCO2 "Nuclear-Topping" Cycle Architecture enabled by FDAA Fractal Heat Exchangers

Abstract: This paper presents the design and thermodynamic modeling of a hybrid Supercritical CO2 (sCO2) power cycle, specifically engineered for the retrofit and modernization of existing Pressurized Water Reactors (PWR).

Current PWRs face a thermodynamic bottleneck: their cold source temperature is limited to approximately 325°C, which is insufficient to unlock the high efficiencies of sCO2 cycles (which require >500°C). To overcome this limit without modifying the reactor core, we propose a "Nuclear-Topping" architecture:

  1. Base Preheating (Nuclear): The reactor heat raises the fluid temperature up to 300°C.

  2. Peak Superheating (External Source): A flexible low-carbon source (hydrogen, green electricity, thermal storage) boosts the fluid to 500°C.

The enabling technology for this architecture is the FDAA (Fractal Density Activation Axiom) formalism applied to heat exchanger design. We introduce the "Still-Fish" fractal geometry, characterized by a specific spectral dimension Ds = 5/8 and a radial dimension Dx = 17/8. This topology aligns vorticity with the flow, achieving a 67% reduction in pressure drop and a 130% increase in heat transfer compared to conventional zigzag channels.

Crucially, the fractal geometry allows for extreme compactness (-70% volume), making it physically possible to integrate the superheating stage within the constrained space of existing reactor containment buildings.

Key Results:

  • Net Efficiency: 46% (compared to 33% for current steam cycles).

  • Power Gain: +126 MWe net flexible power per 900 MWe unit.

  • Flexibility: Transforms baseload nuclear plants into hybrid units capable of load following and renewable energy integration.

  • Economics: Estimated Return on Investment (ROI) of 5 to 6 years, driven by the valuation of peaking capacity.
metadata.method:
Titre : Architecture de Cycle Hybride sCO2 "Nuclear-Topping" par Intégration d'Échangeurs Fractals FDAA

Résumé : Ce document détaille la conception et la modélisation thermodynamique d'un cycle de puissance hybride au CO2 supercritique (sCO2), conçu pour la modernisation des centrales nucléaires à eau pressurisée (REP).

Le verrou technologique actuel réside dans la température de source froide des REP (limitée à environ 325°C), insuffisante pour atteindre les rendements élevés du sCO2 (>500°C). Pour contourner cette limite thermodynamique sans modifier le cœur du réacteur, nous proposons une architecture "Nuclear-Topping" (Surchauffe Nucléaire Hybride) :

  1. Préchauffage Base (Nucléaire) : La chaleur du réacteur assure l'élévation de température jusqu'à 300°C.

  2. Surchauffe Pointe (Source Externe) : Une source décarbonée flexible (hydrogène, électricité verte, stockage thermique) porte le fluide à 500°C.

L'innovation centrale repose sur l'utilisation du formalisme FDAA (Fractal Density Activation Axiom) pour la conception des échangeurs. La géométrie fractale "Still-Fish" (dimension spectrale Ds = 5/8 et dimension radiale Dx = 17/8) permet une compacité extrême (-70% de volume par rapport aux échangeurs tubulaires classiques). Cette densité de puissance est la condition sine qua non pour intégrer l'étage de surchauffe dans l'espace contraint des bâtiments réacteurs existants (rétrofit).

Résultats clés :

  • Rendement net : 46% (contre 33% pour les cycles vapeur actuels).

  • Gain de puissance : +126 MWe nets pilotables par tranche de 900 MWe.

  • Flexibilité : Conversion des centrales de base en unités hybrides capables de suivi de charge et de valorisation des ENR.

  • Viabilité économique : Temps de retour sur investissement estimé entre 5 et 6 ans grâce à la valorisation de la capacité de pointe.
